newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope has appendix removed, no problems.
newsitem.headline: Pope has appendix removed, no problems.

text.p: Pope John Paul had a two-hour operation on Tuesday to remove his appendix, hospital sources said, and Italian news agencies said the surgery was performed without a hitch.

A reporter saw the 76-year-old Pope, attached to a drip, being wheeled on a bed back to his special 10th floor suite of Rome's Gemelli hospital surrounded by doctors and guards after emerging from the operating theatre on the floor below.

He had appeared relaxed and smiled at security officers and nurses he passed on his way into the operating theatre shortly after 7 a.m. (0500 GMT) following prayers in the chapel of his suite, a member of his entourage said.
Barring complications, the Pope is expected to stay in hospital for about five days prior to convalescence.
The ANSA news agency, quoting hospital sources, said the operation, conducted by the same surgeon who saved the Pope's life after he was shot in 1981, ended shortly before 9.00 a.m.
It said the Pope had awoken from anaesthetic at around 9.10 a.m. and that the operation had been "carried out without complications". The AGI news agency carried a similar report.
Neither dispatch could immediately be confirmed. An official medical bulletin was expected to be issued at around 11 a.m. (0900 GMT).

The Vatican announced plans for the operation last month when it said recurrent inflammation of the appendix was the cause of three bouts of "intestinal fever" the Pope has suffered since last Christmas.

The announcement has failed to quell intense speculation that the Polish-born Pope may be suffering from a new tumour, a theory dismissed by the Vatican as "medical fiction" when the Pope entered the Gemelli on Sunday.

It has not specifically denied reports that the Pope also has Parkinson's Disease. The neurological disorder can be marked by the sort of violent trembling that has become increasingly apparent in the Pope's left hand.
The Pope, who has asked the world's 960 million Roman Catholics to pray for him, is being treated at the Gemelli by a team made up of some of Rome's leading doctors.
It is led by Professor Francesco Crucitti, the surgeon who saved the Pope's life in May 1981 after he was shot by Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca in St Peter's Square.
Crucitti operated on the Pope again in 1981 and in July 1992, when a tumour the size of an orange was removed from his colon as it was starting to turn malignant.
The Pope also had hip replacement surgery at the Gemelli in 1994 after breaking his right leg in a bathroom fall.
The Pontiff, who this month celebrates 18 years as leader of the world's Roman Catholics, had a battery of preparatory tests on Monday ahead of surgery.
Doctors said he was patient and calm as he underwent the examinations, including blood and urine tests, an electrocardiogram, an echo-doppler to monitor the quality of blood flow and a chest X-ray.
The chief cardiologist on the medical team, Professor Attilio Maseri, pronounced the Pope's heart completely fit.
The "Pilgrim Pope" has repeatedly said he wants to lead the Catholic Church into the third millennium and has kept up a punishing schedule despite frequently appearing to be in pain.
Polish Cardinal Jozef Glemp told Vatican Radio on Monday evening he hoped the Pope "can quickly return to his mission and next year take his awaited trip to Poland".
